```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

Latent transition analysis (LTA) estimates latent states at successive
occasions and the probabilities of transitions between them. In the default
model, profiles have a common measurement definition across occasions.
With latent group classes, initial-state probabilities and transition
matrices differ by class, representing heterogeneity in longitudinal
patterns.

## Data

`course_engagement` is simulated and has one row per course enrolment: 1,422 enrolments from
106 students. `lta()` needs three kinds of variables.

- **Group:** `student` identifies whose occasions belong together.
- **Occasion order:** `sequence` is the position of each course in the
  student's history. Students can have different numbers of occasions.
- **Indicators:** five activity measures (`browse`, `lectures`, `forum_read`,
  `forum_post`, `attendance`), each standardized within course, so 0 is the
  course average.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
```

## Fit

The `lta()` function requires indicators (`vars`), a group identifier
(`id`), and occasion order (`time`). The arguments `n_profiles` and
`n_group_classes` specify the latent structure; `n_starts` and `seed`
control repeated estimation from reproducible starting values.

```{r fit}
moves <- lta(course_engagement,
             vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post",
                      "attendance"),
             id = "student", time = "sequence",
             n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
moves
```

The `"starts"` table reports the log likelihood reached by each start.
Replication of the selected likelihood supports numerical stability but
does not establish that the global maximum has been found.

```{r starts}
get_results(moves, "starts")
```

## Profiles

The profile plot displays estimated indicator means and the estimated share
of occasions in each profile. For a transition model, `plot()` without an
explicit view instead displays transition matrices.

```{r profiles}
plot_profiles(moves)
```

The profile heatmap expresses each mean in standard deviations from the
indicator's overall mean, facilitating comparison across indicators.

```{r heatmap}
plot_profiles(moves, what = "heatmap")
```

## Starting probabilities

The `"initial"` table reports initial profile probabilities (`probability`),
profile prevalence across occasions (`prevalence`), and estimated group-class
proportions (`group_class_probability`).

```{r initial}
get_results(moves, "initial")
```

## Transitions

The `"transitions"` table reports the probability of moving from state
`from` to state `to` at the next occasion. Probabilities sum to one within
each origin state and group class. The column `stable` identifies transitions
that retain the same state; `expected_count` reports the posterior expected
transition count. A row with `estimated = FALSE` lacks information for
estimating that transition distribution.

```{r transitions}
get_results(moves, "transitions")
```

The transition plot displays one matrix per group class, with current
profiles in rows and next-occasion profiles in columns.

```{r transition-plot}
plot_transitions(moves)
```

## Sequences

The sequence plot displays one row per group, coloured by the most probable
profile at each occasion. These modal assignments summarize the fitted
sequences but omit classification uncertainty.

```{r sequences, fig.height = 6}
plot_sequences(moves)
```

## Classification

The `"entropy"` table reports relative entropy for occasions and groups.
With more than one class, a value of 1 indicates certain posterior membership;
0 indicates equal posterior probabilities across classes for every case.
Entropy summarizes classification separation under the fitted model.

```{r entropy}
get_results(moves, "entropy")
```

Diagnostic plots display per-case uncertainty within each profile
(`what = "entropy"`) and posterior probabilities of assigned profiles
(`what = "posteriors"`).

```{r entropy-plot}
plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "entropy")
```

```{r posteriors-plot}
plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "posteriors")
```

## Transition networks

The estimated transitions can be represented as networks. `get_tna()`
returns a network pooled across group classes; `get_group_tna()` returns one
network per class. Both functions produce
[tna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tna) objects that can be displayed
with `plot()`.

```{r networks, message = FALSE, eval = requireNamespace("tna", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(get_tna(moves))
plot(get_group_tna(moves))
```

## Beyond homogeneous transitions

Several extensions permit alternative specifications of temporal dependence
and measurement:

- `transition_covariates` lets covariates shift the transition
  probabilities: the log odds of moving to each other profile rather than
  staying. A covariate may change over occasions.
- `initial_covariates` lets covariates shift the starting profile.
- `transitions = "occasion"` estimates a separate transition matrix for each
  move.
- `measurement = "occasion"` lets the profiles' means and variances differ by
  occasion.
- `order = 2` makes the next profile depend on the two previous ones.
- `mover_stayer = TRUE` adds a class of groups that never change profile.

`enumerate_classes(..., time = "sequence")` compares numbers of profiles and
group classes, and `bootstrap_lrt()` tests a model against a nested one.

The following example examines whether `previous_grade`, which varies
across courses, is associated with transition probabilities:

```{r grade}
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
homogeneous <- lta(course_engagement, activity, "student", n_profiles = 2,
                   time = "sequence", seed = 1)
grade <- lta(course_engagement, activity, "student", n_profiles = 2,
             time = "sequence", transition_covariates = "previous_grade",
             seed = 1)
get_results(grade, "transition_coefficients")
```

The estimated odds ratios are close to one, and the confidence intervals for
the log-odds coefficients include zero. These results provide limited
evidence of an association between previous grade and transitions in this
example; they do not establish the absence of an association. A second-order
model, in which the next profile depends on the two previous states, can also
be compared with the first-order specification using BIC:

```{r second-order}
second <- lta(course_engagement, activity, "student", n_profiles = 2,
              time = "sequence", order = 2, seed = 1)
BIC(homogeneous, grade, second)
```

```{r check-extensions, include = FALSE}
slopes <- subset(get_results(grade, "transition_coefficients"),
                 term == "previous_grade")
stopifnot(all(slopes$conf_low < 0 & slopes$conf_high > 0),
          BIC(homogeneous) < BIC(grade), BIC(homogeneous) < BIC(second))
```

For these data, BIC is lower for the homogeneous first-order model than for
either extension. Extended models provide transition and initial-state logit
coefficients, with Wald standard errors when supported by the fitted model,
and occasion-specific probability summaries.

## Assumptions

- By default the next profile depends only on the current profile and the
  group class, and transition probabilities are the same at every occasion;
  the arguments above relax each of these.
- Profiles have the same definition at every occasion unless
  `measurement = "occasion"`.
- Indicators are independent within a profile (the default diagonal
  covariance; `covariance_model = "full"` or a non-diagonal `model` relaxes it).

```{r restore-options, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
